thread.title: PayPal (PYPL) 3rd Quarter Earnings: What to Expect

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: PayPal (PYPL) 3rd Quarter Earnings: What to Expect
text:
Shutterstock photo
There’s a war on payments — one that is being fought by the likes of tech giants Apple ( AAPL ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) and Square ( SQ ) as they race to make cash irrelevant not only for retail transactions, but also in high growth areas such as person-to-person payments.
Investors want to know where PayPal ( PYPL ), which has quickly established a strong execution track record since it was spun out from e-commerce giant eBay ( EBAY ) in July 2015, fits in that scenario. The fintech pioneer is set to report third quarter fiscal 2018 earnings results after the closing bell Thursday.
For the three months that ended September, PayPal is expected to earn 54 cents per share on revenue of $3.66 billion. This compared to the year-ago quarter when the company earned 46 cents per share on revenue of $3.24 billion. For the full year, ending in December, earnings are projected to rise 23% year over year to $2.34 per share, while full-year revenue of $15.42 billion would mark a rise of 17.8% year over year.
PayPal has emerge as the trusted fintech arm for traditional financiers such as Citigroup ( C ), JPMorgan ( JPM ) and Visa ( V ), which don’t want to get left behind. PayPal is also taking major steps toward monetizing its popular Venmo app, which gets a cut of each consumer transaction. Users pay 25 cents to transfer monies received via Venmo to their bank accounts. Plus, the company last quarter said some 17% of Venmo users have engaged in a “monetized experience” since launch.
On Thursday investors will be eager to get more details regarding the number of users that are on Venmo and to what extent has the product benefited from their “monetized experience,” which — if successful — can sustain PayPal’s revenue growth for years to come. This was a point made recently by Jefferies analyst John Hecht, who rates PayPal stock with a Buy with a $110 price target.
But PayPal shares, which closed Wednesday at $80.09, don’t fully reflect this sentiment. While the stock has risen 8.79% year to date, that still reflects a 15% pullback from its 52-week high of $93.70. Notably, the stock has corrected even as PayPal delivered six straight earnings and revenue beats. To get the stock going again, on Thursday, not only must PayPal demonstrate sustained growth in payment volumes, a strong increase in customer accounts is a must.
Elsewhere, investors could get excited about potential M&A announcements that would be perceived as accretive to profits. The company earlier this year acquired iZettle — a competitor to Square — that makes hardware that accepts card payments. Any update regarding synergies and-or future deals would be well-received. All told, while the payments space has become crowded, PayPal should remain among the leaders in the foreseeable future, given the moat the company has established.
